title: By Killing Khamenei, the West Created a Martyr – and Mainstream Media Is Ignoring the Muslim Backlash

in Tehran attend a memorial vigil after the assassination of Ayatollah Ali
Khamenei on March 1, 2026. Photo by Majid Saeedi/Getty Images_

When Israeli and American forces killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei [in strikes on
his office](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/28/satellite-imagery-of-
devastation-at-iranian-supreme-leaders-residence-00805793), they didn't just
eliminate a political leader. They created a martyr with reach far beyond
Iran's borders - and triggered a backlash that Western media is barely
covering.

The [protests](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/2/fury-on-pakistan-
streets-20-dead-after-us-israel-strike-kills-khamenei) erupting across the
[Muslim world](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/1/world-reacts-to-
killing-of-irans-khamenei-by-us-israel-forces), the attacks on US embassies
and consulates from Pakistan to Lebanon to Iraq, the mass demonstrations in
cities from Karachi to
[Baghdad](https://www.aljazeera.com/video/newsfeed/2026/3/2/raqi-police-
disperse-pro-iran-protesters-near-us-embassy) to
[Lucknow](https://indianexpress.com/article/cities/lucknow/old-lucknow-to-
protest-ayatollah-khameneis-death-10559091/) to Beirut - these aren't just
about geopolitics. They're about the killing of a religious authority whose
significance transcends national politics.

Hezbollah [fired rockets](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israel-
strikes-lebanon-following-hezbollah-attacks-widening-iran-
conflict-2026-03-02/) at Israel on Monday and officially entered the conflict,
[explicitly citing Khamenei's
killing](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/2/hezbollah-promises-to-
confront-us-israel-over-khamenei-killing). They've opened another front in a
war that's already spiraling beyond anyone's control.

Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was not Nicolas Maduro. He was not Saddam Hussein. He
was not Muammar Gaddafi. Understanding the difference matters enormously for
what comes next.

### The Spiritual Dimension

Khamenei held the title of supreme leader, but his authority derived from his
position as a marja - a source of emulation in Shia Islam. For millions of
Shia Muslims globally, he wasn't just a political figure. He was a religious
guide whose rulings on Islamic law shaped daily life, whose interpretations of
faith carried spiritual weight.

This is a role Western political frameworks struggle to comprehend. Imagine if
the Pope were also head of state of a large country - and then assassinated by
a military strike. The outrage wouldn't be limited to Vatican City. It would
reverberate through Catholic communities worldwide, regardless of their
politics.

Khamenei's followers span Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bahrain,
Yemen, and Shia communities across the Gulf, South Asia, and beyond. Millions
who never supported the Islamic Republic's domestic policies still viewed him
as a religious authority. His Friday prayers were broadcast globally. His
fatwas on everything from finance to family law guided believers.

By killing him, the US and Israel didn't just strike Iran's government. They
struck a spiritual leader with transnational religious authority - and created
exactly the kind of martyr that galvanizes movements for generations.

### The Backlash We're Not Seeing Covered

Mainstream Western media is focusing almost exclusively on what happens inside
Iran. Who replaces Khamenei? Will there be internal fracturing? Can this
weaken the Islamic Republic?

What's missing is the regional explosion already underway.

US embassies in Pakistan and Iraq have been
[attacked](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/mar/01/people-dead-after-
pro-iran-protests-pakistan-iraq). In Lebanon, Hezbollah has opened a new front
explicitly in response to Khamenei's assassination. In Bahrain, where a Shia
majority is ruled by a Sunni monarchy backed by Saudi Arabia and the US,
demonstrations are being met with violent crackdowns. Yemen and parts of India
with significant Shia populations are seeing solidarity protests.

This isn't coordinated by the Iranian government - it's organic rage at the
killing of a religious figure many viewed as a legitimate spiritual authority,
compounded by decades of US military intervention in Muslim-majority
countries. The attacks on American diplomatic facilities aren't aberrations.
They're predictable responses to what millions see as the assassination of a
religious leader by the same powers that have waged war across the region for
over 25 years.

### Complexity and Consequences

Khamenei has many supporters inside Iran, as was seen in the crowds of people
who gathered across the country to mourn the supreme leader. But he was deeply
controversial and also had a lot of detractors. He presided over decades of
[political repression inside Iran](https://www.amnesty.org/en/location/middle-
east-and-north-africa/middle-east/iran/report-iran/). Protesters were killed,
activists imprisoned, dissent crushed in the name of preserving the
revolution. Many Iranians - in the diaspora and inside the country - [feel
relief at his death](https://www.cnn.com/2026/03/01/middleeast/iranians-
future-leader-tehran-khamenei). But relief at the end of an authoritarian
ruler doesn't mean acceptance of assassination by foreign powers. Many
Iranians who opposed Khamenei's rule are still not okay with their leader
being killed by the US and Israel. That distinction matters.

And globally, the spiritual dimension changes everything. This wasn't a
political decapitation strike like so many others. It was the killing of a
marja whose religious authority extended far beyond Iran's borders, whose
martyrdom at 86 by the forces he defined his life fighting against
immortalizes his legacy in ways his aging rule never could.

The US and Israel may have calculated that this would weaken Iran. What
they've actually done is create a martyr, inflame the broader Muslim world,
open new fronts in an expanding regional war, and demonstrate - again - that
decapitation strikes don't produce the outcomes they claim to want.

Iran is not run by one man. The Islamic Republic has institutional depth and
succession mechanisms. But now it also has a martyred supreme leader whose
death will be invoked for decades as proof of Western aggression against Islam
itself - and whose killing has already brought Hezbollah into direct
confrontation with Israel.

Watch the streets of Karachi, Beirut, Baghdad, and Manama. Watch the rocket
fire from Lebanon. That's where the real consequences of this assassination
are unfolding--and Western media is barely looking.

_**Narges Bajoghli** is an anthropologist and associate professor of Middle
East Studies at Johns Hopkins University's School of Advanced International
Studies. She is the author of multiple books on Iranian politics and society._
